pr_title: Adding generation of substitution files for trimming out resources when feature switch is present
pr_body:
Contributes to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/34057
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/37587

cc: @eerhardt @tarekgh 

These changes will make it such that all of the assemblies we ship which also have resources will no also contain a Substitutions file embedded such that if the user selects either the appContext switch or sets a property (that needs to be defined and added on the linker targets) on the project, then all resources will be removed and only resource keys will be used instead. I'm waiting on an arcade change in order to be able to add tests for this which will make sure that setting the runtimeconfig switch will cause this to happen but that will be added into this PR.

FYI: @danmosemsft @vitek-karas @marek-safar

issue_context.title: SR.GetResourceString doesn't return resource key when UsingResourceKeys is true
issue_context.body:
`SR.UsingResourceKeys` is a property meant to be set to true if the resources should not report full resource strings, but instead just the resource key itself. This is used for example in .NET Native but we now plan to potentially use it when trimming apps in .NET Core well. The advantage of doing this is that the tooling can remove the relatively large string resources and thus reduce the size of an app.

The intent of this feature was to use the resource key value instead of the resource string for an error message. So for example instead of: "Value cannot be null" it should return "ArgumentNull_Generic".

Unfortunately the code currently returns empty strings only. This is because the `System.SR.GetResourceString(string)` overload calls `GetResourceString(resourceKey, string.Empty);` but the implementation of that will only return the `resourceKey` if the second parameter is `null` - which in this case pretty much never is. Otherwise it returns he second parameter which is always null.
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @tarekgh, @buyaa-n, @krwq
Notify danmosemsft if you want to be subscribed.

I think this issue only applies to System.Private.CoreLib, right?

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/bd6cbe3642f51d70839912a6a666e5de747ad581/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/SR.cs#L21-L25

That method is only complied in for CoreLib, all the other libraries don't have it.

Is the fix here simply to change `string.Empty` to `null`? Normally I would think we could just remove the method altogether, but the comment `Needed for debugger integration` makes me hesitant to do that. I wonder what "debugger integration" is happening with this method?

I'm hesitant about the change to `null`. The default value is used even when we're not in the trimmed scenario - in that case it's used as a fallback if the resource key can't be found. So it's probably better to leave it an empty string (so that the API never returns null) and instead detect empty string as the "special" value.

I don't know anything about the debugger comment.

/cc @MichalStrehovsky
Maybe @tarekgh would know about resources and `#if !DEBUGRESOURCES`?

Our build tools (when compiling a library in .NET Native) used to include all resource strings as literal strings inside the code and have `DEBUGRESOURCES` def to enable these strings. This is done in debug builds only. So if you use the debug build of the library the method `GetResourceString(resourceKey, string)` will pass the second parameter the resource literal string. This was done to help to get the full resource strings when using the debug builds. I don't think our build tools still producing this in debug builds in our runtime repo.

Looking at the whole things here, in .NET Native we used to override UsingResourceKeys value through the IL transformers and turn it true during the library compilation. I don't think we are doing any of that in runtime anyway. so all logic can be removed if the linker work is not going to use it. Please advise how you think the linker will work and we can decide what needs to be done here.

@tarekgh The goal is for linker to do basically exactly what .NET Native did - we're going to overwrite the `UsingResourceKeys` to return `true`. That's how I found about the weird behavior - I made linker to overwrite the method and tried to run a simple app which printed out an error message for `ArgumentNullException`.

Before change it prints out:
```
System.ArgumentNullException: Value cannot be null. (Parameter 'args')
```

After change:
```
System.ArgumentNullException:  , args
```

The expected output based on the intent of the code should look like:
```
System.ArgumentNullException: ArgumentNull_Generic Arg_ParamName_Name, args
```

I have traced the change that introduced the comment `Needed for debugger integration` and using `String.Empty` to the commit https://github.com/dotnet/corert/commit/455c8c0d1c9e77403a112ee0475f202c4186da18. I believe these changes were only specific to .NET Native to enable better-debugging experience but I don't think there is a real (VS/WinDBG) debugger integration.

Considering that, I would say, we can go ahead and unify the usage of SR.cs between the libraries and corelib and use `null` instead of `String.Empty`
